name: Gustav Lindahl
languages: Norwegian (near enough, he says, and the Norwegians disagree)
equipment: Leather duster, black, over a black frock coat whose elbows his landlady has patched twice
Navy revolver (Colt, .36), 6 chambers loaded, which he carries because a man must, and has fired at nothing but snakes
Pick handle, which he calls his crook and leans on as a walking stick
A Swedish Bible with his father's name in the front, and an English one with his own
A school bell, a box of slates, chalk, and twelve copies of McGuffey's Third Reader belonging to the Bitter Creek school district
A small leather case with bandages, carbolic, laudanum and a pair of forceps, because there is only one doctor in the county
Mule: Ezekiel, grey, who is wiser than he is
Saddle, bedroll, slicker, a canteen and a coffee pot
A pocket hymnal, a pencil and a notebook of sermons he has never preached because they were too angry
features: Two Tongues (Immigrant origin: speaks Swedish and English fluently and one more language well; advantage on Insight and Perception checks to follow a conversation held in a language the speakers assume he doesn't know; among people who share one of his languages he finds a meal, a bed, work and the news without a check)

Fire and Brimstone (Preacher, WIS: as an action he preaches, words only and no miracle: Steady, each ally within 30 ft who can hear him gains 1d6 + 3 temporary hit points and the frightened and Shaken conditions end; or Shake, each enemy within 30 ft who can hear and understand him makes a WIS save, DC 13, or is frightened of him until the end of his next turn; 3 uses, regained on a short or long rest)

Comfort the Afflicted (Preacher: he can stabilise a dying creature as a bonus action with a DC 10 Medicine check, and it regains 1 hit point; once per long rest, ten minutes with someone grieving, frightened or ashamed ends the Shaken condition and he learns what truly troubles them)

The Flock (Preacher, 2nd level: wherever there is a church, a camp meeting or a gathering of decent people he finds shelter, a meal, news and a few people who will speak for him; once per town, an hour's preaching gives him a temporary +1 Reputation there, or -1 to someone he preaches against by name, if the crowd believes him)

The Schoolhouse (Schoolteacher background: the families of the creek, Company and grange alike, trust him with what they would not tell the sheriff, and their children, who see everything, tell him what their parents won't; he can read and write any document in English or Swedish)

personality.traits: I speak slowly, in good careful English with a Swedish tune to it, and I quote scripture only when I cannot help it. I am gentle with children, the sick and the drunk, and patient with everyone except the comfortable.
personality.ideals: Every soul on this creek, cowboy or homesteader, is worth the same to God, and I mean to behave as if that were true even when it is inconvenient.
personality.bonds: My school, eleven children in a log room by the grange hall. The Company's cowboys, to whom I preach on alternate Sundays in the bunkhouse at the Forks, and who listen. And Owen Lasker, whom I am to bury on Wednesday.
personality.flaws: I am on the Association's dead list as 'the Swede preacher', for preaching against it, and I am afraid. I have a temper I keep in a box, and when the lid comes off I am not a Christian at all.

appearance: A lanky, stooped, flaxen man of thirty-eight with a long, plain, kind face, pale eyebrows, steel spectacles, big bony hands and a voice that can fill a grange hall without his seeming to raise it. Black frock coat, black duster, a wide black hat, and a grey mule that does not like to be hurried.
backstory: Gustav Lindahl was the son of a Lutheran pastor in Småland, trained for the ministry at Uppsala, and in 1876, at twenty-eight, emigrated to Minnesota after a quarrel with his bishop about whether a farmhand's soul was worth as much as a landowner's. He taught school in a Swedish settlement there for six years, and in 1883 followed a wagon train of Scandinavian homesteaders west to Bitter Creek as their schoolmaster and, because no ordained minister would come, their preacher. He is not ordained in America and does not pretend to be. He teaches the creek's children their letters in a log schoolroom by the grange hall, Company children and grange children together, and on alternate Sundays he rides twenty-eight miles to the Forks and preaches to the Company's cowboys in the bunkhouse, because, he says, nobody else will, and Wade Tolliver allows it. Last autumn he preached a sermon against the dead list in the grange hall and the next week his name was on it. Owen Lasker was one of his parishioners and his friend; Owen taught him to read a survey map, and he taught Owen to read Swedish. On Monday Thea asks him to bury Owen on Wednesday. On Monday night, at the Antelope, a frightened boy called Ira Pettit will not meet his eyes. (Suggested employer: the grange, or the widow. Hooks into the Company: his bunkhouse congregation, Wade Tolliver's respect, and the children of both sides.)
